title: Inspecting and Testing Data Types
keywords: data types, casting, and type promotion
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of inspecting and testing data types and name one situation where it is useful.
Apply np.issubdtype() to a small NumPy example and inspect the resulting values, shape, or dtype.
Identify one important limitation, boundary case, or validation check for inspecting and testing data types.

content.intro: This lesson develops topic 64 of the supplied curriculum: **Inspecting and Testing Data Types**. The main starting point is **np.issubdtype()**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: A dtype controls range, precision, storage, and which operations are valid. Casting should be explicit when loss, overflow, or NumPy 2.x promotion behavior matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Inspecting and Testing Data Types** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **np.issubdtype()** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

content_blocks.code:
import numpy as np

values = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.issubdtype(values.dtype, np.integer))

Observed output in the available validation environment (Python 3.13.5, NumPy 2.3.5):

common_mistakes.why: Float-to-integer conversion truncates and narrower dtypes may overflow.
common_mistakes.fix: Check input ranges and precision requirements before casting.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming mixed types promote the same way in every version
common_mistakes.why: NumPy 2.x promotion semantics differ from some older code.
common_mistakes.fix: Test mixed-type operations and consult the migration guide.
